strategy_name: Dual / Triple moving-average crossover (always-in-market)
mechanism: A fast MA crossing a slow MA defines trend state; being always in the market removes discretion and captures every sustained move; the book's tests show the simplest version (Dual MA) beat the more complex filtered version (Triple MA)
setup_summary: Dual MA: long when 100-day MA > 350-day MA, short when below; always in the market, exit = flip. Triple MA: 150/250-day crossover gated by the 350-day trend filter; not always in the market. Results (Table 10-1): Dual MA CAGR 57.8%, MAR 1.82 (best MAR of all six systems), Sharpe 1.55; Triple MA 48.1%, MAR 1.53 - complexity did not help. No stops in either; adding stops made every metric worse.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: fast MA crosses slow MA (or the pair crosses the filter MA). Invalidation: the crossing back - the position flips rather than exits to flat.
risk_geometry: entry: next-bar open on crossover; stop: none; target: none; expiry: none - the system is always long or short, so exposure is continuous.
quote: This is a very simple system that buys and sells when a 100-day moving average crosses over a slower 350-day moving average. Unlike the other systems, this system is always in the market, either long or short.
chapter_anchor: Ch.10 Turtle-Style Trading: Step by Step, Dual & Triple Moving Average (pp.141-144)
notes: Backtested in the book (1996-2006) - falsifiable and corroborated across the trend-following literature. Perp caveat: 'always in the market' means paying (or earning) funding continuously, so net carry drag is a real, testable term that does not exist in futures; on 1h bars, 100/350 MA needs ~2-3 weeks warm-up. The 'simpler beat complex' result reinforces V8 rule 14's simplicity budget and the frozen-OOS screening approach.
book: Way of the Turtle - The Secret Methods that Turned Ordinary People into Legendary Traders 2007

strategy_name: Trader effects: visible signal crowding and front-running
mechanism: A rule-based signal that is publicly known (e.g., breakout levels) gets front-run and diluted: other traders trade ahead of the triggering orders, changing what the signal means and eroding or destroying the edge; conversely, unappealing strategies (high drawdown) have long lifetimes
setup_summary: The gold example (pp.154-156): a trader who knows a 1,000-lot buy order sits at $410.50 buys ahead, pushes price to the trigger, sells into the breakout buyers, net +$160K. Mechanism: edges decay as capital flows into them - the popular breakout system in the book drew hundreds of millions in AUM and then produced its worst 20-year drawdown. Mitigations: use limit orders (not market), keep signals private, avoid optimizing to public/illiquid markets; the Turtles varied stops/entry timing to obfuscate.
trigger_invalidation: N/A - a backtest-degradation and execution methodology; relevant when a candidate edge is widely known or machine-monitorable.
risk_geometry: Execution layer: limit/stop orders rather than market orders; entry closer to the touch; avoid illiquid venues (lumber/propane style small markets) where anticipatory orders move price.
quote: If too many traders start to try to take advantage of a particular strategy, that strategy will cease working as well as it did previously.
chapter_anchor: Ch.11 Lies, Damn Lies, and Backtests, Trader Effects (pp.153-158); also Ch.10 (pp.144, 147)
notes: Most relevant methodology for crypto: Donchian-style levels are public, machine-monitored, and stop-huntable on perp order books, so any formalized V8 expert should assume front-running of visible thresholds (supports V8's point-in-time MarketState and frozen refs - and argues against broadcasting live signal levels). Also explains the book's observation that Donchian's edge decayed vs the Turtle era, and that trader effects can arise without conscious collusion.
book: Way of the Turtle - The Secret Methods that Turned Ordinary People into Legendary Traders 2007

strategy_name: Drawdown clustering: correlated bad days at trend ends (Monte Carlo with chunk scrambling)
mechanism: At the end of large trends, markets that are usually uncorrelated move against everyone at once and bad days are serially correlated; Monte Carlo that scrambles individual trades (or single-day changes) destroys this clustering and understates drawdowns, so validation must scramble in multi-day chunks
setup_summary: When simulating alternative equity paths, trade-scrambling MC removes the date-link between correlated markets (gold+silver+sugar all down mid-May to mid-June 2006) and understates drawdown magnitude/frequency; equity-curve scrambling with 20-day chunks preserves the serial correlation of daily net changes. The Oct 1987 eurodollar gap and the 'everything moves against you at once' behavior are the motivating evidence. Robust measures (RAR%, R-cubed = RAR%/(length-adjusted avg of 5 largest drawdowns)) are also introduced as less luck-sensitive alternatives to CAGR/MAR/Sharpe.
trigger_invalidation: Validation result invalid if: test period covers only 1-2 market states (like polling only Democrats, Ch.12), sample < ~100 trades (rule triggers with <5 occurrences are uninformative), or parameters sit on a 'cliff' (1% parameter change flips result, e.g., 45.7% to -0.4%).
risk_geometry: N/A - validation and performance-measurement methodology; informs simulator and registry gates rather than trade geometry.
quote: at the end of a large trend when it breaks down and reverses, it seems that everything moves against you at once; even markets that normally do not seem correlated become so on those volatile days when a large trend disintegrates.
chapter_anchor: Ch.12 On Solid Ground, Monte Carlo Simulation (pp.200-205); Ch.8 (p.119); Ch.11 cliffs (pp.173-176)
notes: Crypto perps make this worse, not better: BTC/ETH/alt perps share funding, leverage, and liquidation cascades, so simultaneous bad days are the norm at breakdowns - any V8 Monte Carlo / bootstrap validation must preserve cross-market date alignment and serial correlation (scramble in chunks), or it will understate drawdown. Also supports V8's canonical-L1 simulator retaining correlation structure and its frozen-OOS gates (the optimization paradox - optimized parameters overstate future - is directly relevant to V8's challenger-vs-frozen-OOS rule).
book: Way of the Turtle - The Secret Methods that Turned Ordinary People into Legendary Traders 2007

strategy_name: Hammer and Hanging Man (Umbrella Lines)
mechanism: A long lower shadow with a small real body at the top of the range shows sellers pushed price down during the session but buyers reclaimed the close near the highs; after a downtrend this is seller exhaustion (hammer), after an extended rally it is buyer entrapment that needs confirmation (hanging man).
setup_summary: After a downtrend, a bar whose real body sits at the upper end of the range, lower shadow at least 2x the real body height, and no or very short upper shadow (hammer) is a LONG setup completed at bar close. The identical candle after an extended rally (preferably at an all-time high) is a hanging man: a SHORT setup only once the next bar closes under its real body.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: bar close completes the shape (lower shadow >= 2x body, tiny/absent upper shadow) in the correct trend context; hanging man additionally requires a confirming close under its real body. Invalidation: close under the hammer's low voids support; absence of confirmation after a hanging man keeps the bull trend entrenched (new-high closes negate).
risk_geometry: Entry at hammer close or limit near the lower-shadow support zone; stop under the hammer's low (swing point, ~$5 below in the worked example); candles give no price targets so targets come from Western structure; hanging-man short stop above its high.
quote: It has a long lower shadow that should be at least twice the height of the real body... A hammer must come after a decline. A hanging man must come after a rally.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 4, Reversal Patterns - Umbrella Lines / Hammer / Hanging Man, pp. 32-42
notes: Wick-rejection semantics transfer directly to leveraged BTC; a stop under the wick low is a natural risk_geometry. Overlaps V8's liquidity_sweep_reclaim when the hammer wick takes out a prior extreme; this family covers the pure shape-plus-trend variant. The book's own risk/reward example shows the entry-refinement lesson (buy the correction into the shadow, not the close).
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques 2nd edition 2001 (1)

strategy_name: Dark-Cloud Cover / Piercing Pattern (body-penetration reversals)
mechanism: After a strong one-directional body, the next session opens beyond the prior extreme (gap/opening extension) then closes deep inside the prior body: the extension failed, trapping momentum participants who entered at the open/close and reversing control.
setup_summary: Dark-cloud cover (top): after a strong white body, a black body opens above the prior session's high and closes more than 50% into the white body. Piercing pattern (bottom): after a strong black body, a white body opens below (ideally under) the prior low and closes more than 50% into the black body. Less than 50% penetration is a weaker on-neck/in-neck/thrusting pattern needing next-session confirmation.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: second-bar close penetrating >50% of the first body; dark-cloud's second bar should open above prior high. Invalidation: close back above the pattern high (dark-cloud) / below the pattern low (piercing) voids the reversal; penetration <50% is only a weak signal, not a reversal.
risk_geometry: Entry at pattern-completion close (or wait for bounce to the dark-cloud resistance / pullback to the piercing support for better risk/reward); stop above the highest high of the dark-cloud cover (its resistance anchor) or below the piercing low; greater penetration = higher confidence.
quote: The second day's price opens above the prior session's high... the market closes deeply within the prior day's white body. The greater the degree of penetration into the white real body, the more likely this is a top. Some Japanese technicians require more than a 50-percent penetration.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 4, Reversal Patterns - Dark-Cloud Cover and Piercing Pattern, pp. 49-59
notes: The 'open above prior high' leg maps to gap/opening wicks seen in crypto around liquidation cascades and funding spikes; the >50% body-penetration threshold is a crisp falsifiable parameter. Book admits definitional variance (open above close vs above high) and that non-classic variants can be read by 'how and where' they formed - a subjectivity caveat for machine recognition.
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques 2nd edition 2001 (1)

strategy_name: Morning/Evening Star (three-candle trend exhaustion)
mechanism: A small-body star (gap away from a long one-directional body) reflects a stalemate where the prior trend's force dissipates; the third body closing deep into the first body confirms control has switched.
setup_summary: Morning star (bottom): after a decline, a long black body, then a small real body that does not touch the first body, then a white body intruding deeply into the first body. Evening star (top): mirror after a rally; the star's small body is the first hint of a top. Ideal versions have non-touching real bodies; a doji middle candle = doji star (stronger); double-gap abandoned baby variants are rare but strongest.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: close of the third candle completing the pattern after a trend. Invalidation: a close under the morning star's lowest-low support ref voids the reversal; no preceding trend to reverse = no signal; second and third candles overlapping does not invalidate (gap between them not required).
risk_geometry: Entry at the third-candle close or on a correction back to the pattern's lowest-low support; stop below that low; the book explicitly flags poor risk/reward buying at pattern completion and recommends waiting for the pullback to the support anchor; evening-star resistance = its highs.
quote: The concluding candle of the morning star is a white real body that intrudes deeply into the first session's black candle... The lowest low of the three lines that form this pattern should be support.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 5, Stars - The Morning Star and Evening Star, pp. 62-70
notes: Three-bar patterns complete late (book's own admission), so the operationally actionable part is the pullback-to-support entry, not the completion close. The 'three-river' historical note frames a close over the evening-star resistance / under morning-star support as the confirmation event.
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques 2nd edition 2001 (1)

strategy_name: Doji as Top-Reversal Signal (Northern/Southern doji asymmetry)
mechanism: An open-equals-close session reflects complete bull/bear balance; in an overbought rally this indecision means the buyers' scaffolding gives way (top), but in a downtrend it is a weak bottom signal because an ambivalent market can fall of its own weight.
setup_summary: A doji (open ~= close, any shadows) after a rally, especially after a tall white candle or in an overbought condition, is a potential top: take the highest high between the doji and the prior tall white candle as close-based resistance and require a confirming close under it. Doji in a trading range ('box') has no forecasting implications because there is no trend to reverse.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: doji bar completes in a trending/overbought context. Invalidation: close above the doji-resistance ref negates (market 'refreshed', bullish breakout); a Southern doji (in a decline) is not a bottom signal unless it confirms other support evidence; doji in a box range = no trade; doji with a new high close needs next-session bearish confirmation.
risk_geometry: Resistance = highest high of the doji and prior tall white candle (frozen ref, close-based); stop above it; confirmation = next-session close under the doji's close; doji in a box at range edges merely confirms the range.
quote: The doji is a distinct trend change signal, especially during rallies... as successful as doji are at calling tops, they tend to lose some reversal potential in downtrends... doji have little forecasting implications if they are in a trading range environment since there is no trend to reverse.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 8, The Magic Doji, pp. 155-170
notes: The falsifiable cores are the top/bottom asymmetry claim and the box-range regime filter ('no trend to reverse = no signal'), which doubles as a REGIME_FILTER lesson for all reversal experts. Long-legged/gravestone/dragonfly doji variants are shape refinements of the same family.
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques 2nd edition 2001 (1)

strategy_name: Windows (Gaps) as Support/Resistance with Close-Based Invalidation
mechanism: A price vacuum between two bars (no overlapping shadows) leaves a zone where corrections stop: the window acts as support (rising) or resistance (falling), so the trend continues until the window is closed on a close, not an intraday touch.
setup_summary: A rising window (prior bar's high below current bar's low, shadows not overlapping) in an uptrend is a continuation signal: buy dips toward the window; the whole window is a support zone, critical support is its bottom. Mirror for falling windows (sell bounces, resistance at the top). Trend stays intact - even across many windows - until a close under the last rising window's bottom (or over the last falling window's top); if one window's support breaks, step down to the next window below.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: window bar completes (gap between shadows, size irrelevant - even 4 cents). Invalidation: close under the bottom of a rising window voids the uptrend; close over the top of a falling window voids the downtrend; intraday pierce without a close does not invalidate.
risk_geometry: Entry: buy dips at/near the rising window (aggressive traders may buy near its top); stop: mental or physical on a close under the window bottom; falling-window shorts stop on close over the window top; targets from Western structure.
quote: It is said by Japanese technicians to 'go in the direction of the window'... 'corrections stop at the window.'... If the pullback closes under the bottom of the window, the prior uptrend is voided.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 7, Continuation Patterns - Windows, Tasuki, Gapping Plays, pp. 126-141
notes: Literal gaps between consecutive 1h bars are rare in 24/7 crypto (mostly liquidation/exchange-outage events), lowering signal frequency; but the close-not-intraday invalidation semantics and broken-structure support transfer to V8's lifecycle/simulator rules. Nison himself downplays tasuki/side-by-side variants: 'It is the window that is critical.'
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques 2nd edition 2001 (1)

strategy_name: RSI Divergence + Overbought/Oversold with Candle Confirmation
mechanism: momentum_divergence - price making new highs while RSI fails to follow shows the move lacks internal force; the oscillator is only a warning that becomes actionable when a candle pattern confirms the turn.
setup_summary: Negative divergence (price new high, RSI lower than at the prior price high), especially with RSI in the overbought zone (>70) and confirmed by a top candle (e.g., dark-cloud cover), is a SHORT setup. Positive divergence (price new low, RSI higher) with oversold RSI (<30) plus a bottom candle is a LONG setup. Divergence is more meaningful when RSI is in the overbought/oversold region.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: confirming candle after the divergence forms. Invalidation: price continues to new highs/lows with RSI following (divergence resolved); a candle signal without the oscillator warning (or vice versa) is a weaker signal.
risk_geometry: Entry on the confirming candle, not the oscillator alone; stops beyond the extreme of the move; use the candle anchor (e.g., dark-cloud cover high) for stop placement.
quote: A negative, or bearish, divergence occurs when prices are at a new high, but the oscillator is not... I view an overbought or oversold oscillator as only a warning, a clue, with final confirmation coming with a candlestick pattern.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 14, Candles with Oscillators - The Relative Strength Index, pp. 226-229
notes: Oscillator state (RSI band, divergence flag) is a natural response-group feature; the book insists on candle confirmation, so V8 should consume it as a filter/confirmation feature (convergence input) rather than a standalone expert. An oscillator trendline break adds a second negative signal (Exhibit 14.1).
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques 2nd edition 2001 (1)

strategy_name: Moving Average as Support/Resistance with Candle Confirmation
mechanism: trend_continuation - a moving average that repeatedly holds price becomes a live support/resistance ref in a trend; pullbacks to it resume the trend, but only when a candle signal confirms the bounce.
setup_summary: In an uptrend, pullbacks to a previously-validated moving average (popular lengths: 5/9/30/40/65-day; 9-period EMA common in FX) that hold on a close and form a bullish candle (hammer, bullish engulfing) are LONG entries. A close below the MA is bearish; a validated MA broken on a close becomes resistance (polarity).
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: candle confirmation at the MA (e.g., hammer at MA support) after the MA has been validated. Invalidation: a close through the MA in the breakout direction voids the pullback thesis; an unvalidated MA should not be traded as the sole reason.
risk_geometry: Entry on the confirming candle at the MA; stop below the MA or below the candle low; target from Western structure; only trade MAs that have already proven to hold price.
quote: we can then turn our attention to this particular moving average with the idea that retracements should hold the moving average as support... It is much more important to have a candlestick signal confirming a moving average's support or resistance.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 13, Candles with Moving Averages - Using Moving Averages, pp. 217-224
notes: Corroborates V8's existing trend_pullback (ema_fast > ema_slow, close < ema_slow): adds the conditions that the MA be previously validated and that a candle signal confirm the bounce. Golden/dead cross terminology (dual MA crossover) also documented; 'slope up' refinement noted.
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques 2nd edition 2001 (1)

strategy_name: Reversal Signals Only Trade in the Direction of the Major Trend
mechanism: regime_trend_alignment - a reversal signal against the major trend merely liquidates the trend-side position; entering counter-trend risks being run over by the larger flow even if eventually right ('the market is never wrong').
setup_summary: In a bull market, a top-reversal candle signal is used to liquidate longs and to wait for a bullish signal on the correction, not to initiate a short. In a bear market, bottom-reversal signals are buy-candidates only once the major trend turns. This is an admission filter applied before any reversal-signal entry.
trigger_invalidation: Applies as a filter: the major-trend definition must be explicit (price vs MA, higher lows/higher highs); invalidation of the trend itself re-enables counter-trend signals. Combined with the book's 'If...then system' discipline - stay in the position only if the market behaves as anticipated, otherwise exit.
risk_geometry: NONE - an admission/exit filter (RiskGate style), not a directional strategy; also covered by the book's DISCIPLINE rules (stops always, lose the opinion not the money, pace trades to market environment).
quote: An important principle is to initiate a new position (based on a reversal signal) only if that signal is in the direction of the major trend... This bearish signal would not warrant a short sale... It would, however, signal a liquidation of longs.
chapter_anchor: Chapter 4, Reversal Patterns - introduction, pp. 31-32; DISCIPLINE rules, p. 185
notes: Maps directly onto V8's risk/lifecycle layer (RiskGate admission, one exposure per direction, dead-thesis exits) and the 'market is never wrong' discipline: a stop/exit rule rather than an entry generator. Corroborates the protective-stops sidebar ('A stop should be placed at the time of the original trade... There is no room for hope in the market').
book: Japanese Candlestick Charting Techniques 2nd edition 2001 (1)

strategy_name: Sector relative-strength rotation (top-down ETF selection)
mechanism: Persistent relative strength is created by institutional sector rotation; sectors that resist broad-market drawdowns are the first to new highs on a bounce and the last to fall, so buying relative strength and shorting relative weakness both raises upside and lowers downside.
setup_summary: On 60-min or daily percentage-change overlay charts vs a benchmark, find instruments that diverge persistently: sector holds sideways or higher while the broad market drops and outpaces it on bounces (longs), or vice versa (shorts). Never trade instruments moving in lockstep with the benchmark. Confirm with 'relative strength to itself': close in the upper 30% of the intraday range for longs, bottom 30% for shorts; the middle 40% is the 'danger zone'. Buy the leaders, not the laggards within the strong group.
trigger_invalidation: Entry requires persistent divergence plus %-range close position; thesis invalid when the instrument closes in the danger zone (middle 40% of range) or reverts to benchmark parity.
risk_geometry: entry: bar close or final-hour after divergence confirmed; stop below support; target not fixed - trail or sell into resistance; hold weeks to months (book average: several weeks).
quote: Sectors with relative strength often generate double-digit percentage gains even while the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite are mostly unchanged.
chapter_anchor: Ch.4 'Finding Indexes with the Most Relative Strength' + Ch.3 top-down summary; Ch.5 'Buy the Leaders, Not the Laggards'
notes: Cross-coin relative strength (e.g. ETH/BTC leadership, alt rotation) is testable on perp pairs as a cross_market feature, but V8 currently trades a single instrument (BTCUSDT 1h), so this lands as selection methodology and feature input, not a standalone expert.
book: Trading ETFs - Gaining an Edge with Technical Analysis 2nd edition 2012

strategy_name: Broad-market trend confirmation before directional exposure
mechanism: Roughly 85-90% of individual instruments move with the broad market, so trading against an unclearly-defined market regime is the surest way to lose; confirmed-trend regimes favor directional trading while range regimes chop accounts apart.
setup_summary: A trend exists only when the reference index shows 2 higher highs + 2 higher lows (3 anchor points) for an uptrend (or 2 lower highs + 2 lower lows for a downtrend) AND price trades above both 20- and 50-day MAs with the 20-day closer to price and above the 50-day (mirror for downtrend). Multiple recent MA crossovers, or the 50-day trading closer to price than the 20-day, signal a choppy range - declare range-bound and avoid broad-market instruments. For multi-instrument books, require >=2 of 3 major indexes in confirmed trend before trading the broad market; otherwise trade only independently-trending sectors.
trigger_invalidation: Uptrend invalid when a lower low forms below the trendline; trend stability invalid when 20/50 MA crossover clusters appear (range warning).
risk_geometry: N/A - admission gate: determines whether directional exposure is allowed at all, not a per-trade geometry.
quote: Approximately 85 to 90 percent of stocks and ETFs move in the same general direction as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite. Therefore, failure to clearly identify the direction of the broad market's trend before even considering which ETFs to buy or sell short is a surefire way to lose capital.
chapter_anchor: Ch.3 'Determining the Direction of the Broad Market Trend' (trendline test + 20/50-day MA confirmation)
notes: BTC is its own broad market, so the trendline (3-anchor, 2HH/2HL) + MA-alignment filter is directly implementable on BTCUSDT 1h and maps cleanly to a deterministic V8 regime gate on expert admission.
book: Trading ETFs - Gaining an Edge with Technical Analysis 2nd edition 2012

strategy_name: Volume confirmation of breakouts and distribution-day counting
mechanism: Institutions cannot hide their footprint in volume; breakouts and trends lacking volume confirmation fail to follow through, volume leads price (not lags), and 'volume is the one indicator that never lies'.
setup_summary: Require breakouts out of consolidation bases to spike to 200-300% of the instrument's own average daily volume (relative-to-itself, not absolute). Track accumulation days (up on higher volume) vs distribution days (down on higher volume): healthy markets absorb a couple of distribution days per month, but 5+ distribution days end even strong uptrends. Treat trends formed on light volume with caution and expect support breaks without volume confirmation to fail.
trigger_invalidation: Breakout thesis weakens if volume does not confirm; >=5 distribution days in a month invalidates aggressive long exposure; a break of support that fails to follow through on volume is a bear trap (book's Feb-2003 E-mini example).
risk_geometry: entry: breakout bar/session with 2-3x average volume; stops unchanged from setup; no explicit target.
quote: As a rule of thumb, you want to see ETFs breaking out of bases of consolidation on at least 200 percent to 300 percent of their average daily volume levels.
chapter_anchor: Ch.5 'Analyzing Volume' (accumulation/distribution days, 5-day vs 50-day volume MAs, intraday volume comparison)
notes: Perp volume data exists; the relative-volume (vs its own average) framing is the correct 24/7 analog. Feeds the participation feature group and refines breakout-family volume gates.
book: Trading ETFs - Gaining an Edge with Technical Analysis 2nd edition 2012

strategy_name: 200-period MA 'brick wall' and support/resistance polarity flip
mechanism: The long-term MA acts as a magnet that initial tests rarely pierce; each subsequent test weakens it; after a firm break the level flips polarity (prior resistance becomes new support and vice versa).
setup_summary: When price tests the 200-period MA (as support from above or resistance from below), the first test generally holds (book shows 1-5 failed attempts, e.g. $SOX tried 5 times against its 200-week MA); each retest raises the odds of a firm break; a break with confirmed volume signals a trend change and the level becomes the new support/resistance. Used as both entry trigger (MZZ long on 200-day-MA breakout of the inverse ETF) and exit/target (sell first test of 50-day MA resistance, e.g. GLD July-2006 exit).
trigger_invalidation: A decisive high-volume break through the 200-period MA invalidates the 'wall holds' thesis; repeated failed reclaims after a break confirm real reversal (XHB: 4 failed 50-day-MA breakout attempts then success after an undercut).
risk_geometry: entry: on break with volume, or on bounce off level; stop beyond the level; target: next major MA or prior high/low; timeframe-agnostic.
quote: the 200-day MA simply acts like a brick wall whenever a stock, ETF, or index runs into it... Unless the dominant trend is really strong, it generally requires multiple tests of the 200-day MA before a position bursts through.
chapter_anchor: Ch.6 'The 200-Day Moving Average Brick Wall' (IWM, $SOX weekly, MZZ, ONEQ examples)
notes: Level polarity and multi-test weakening are timeframe-agnostic and directly testable on BTCUSDT 1h; belongs in the location feature group and as an exit-target rule for trend families.
book: Trading ETFs - Gaining an Edge with Technical Analysis 2nd edition 2012

strategy_name: Pullback to the fast MA (10-day / hourly 20-MA) in an established strong trend
mechanism: In strong established trends, institutional buying resumes at fast MAs; the strongest instruments pull back only to the fastest MA (often converging with the uptrend line) and power to new highs, rarely reaching slower MAs.
setup_summary: Require an established trend (2 higher highs + 2 higher lows, 3 anchors). Buy the first test of the 10-day MA in a strong uptrend (or the hourly 20-MA as short entry resistance in a downtrend, book's IWM short), especially when the MA converges with the uptrend line; do not buy the very first touch - wait for confirmation on the next-lower timeframe (break of the hourly downslope / prior-day high). Stop below the 20-day MA. If price gaps to the 10-day MA but fails to close the session above it, scratch the trade.
trigger_invalidation: A firm close below the fast MA invalidates the pullback (expects the leg to the 20-day); a firm close below the 20-day MA precedes a steeper correction to the 50-day; entries on the first touch without confirmation stop out frequently.
risk_geometry: entry: test of 10-day MA with confirmation (next-bar or prior-day-high break); stop: below 20-day MA (or below retracement low); target: prior highs / upper trend channel or overhead resistance; expiry: days to weeks.
quote: The strongest ETFs in the market typically pull back to their 10-day MAs and then power ahead to new highs... if an ETF gaps down to the 10-day MA on the open, but fails to close the session above it, you usually want to scratch the trade because the likelihood of a further correction down to the 20-day MA is high.
chapter_anchor: Ch.6 'Ten-Day Moving Average in Strong Trends' (FXI, INP) + Ch.7 'Pullbacks' (XLB 20-day-MA pullback, IWM short at hourly 20-MA)
notes: V8's trend_pullback expert (ema_fast>ema_slow and close<ema_slow) is corroborated; this refines the entry to a faster-MA pullback with a scratch rule on close below the fast MA and stop below the slower MA.
book: Trading ETFs - Gaining an Edge with Technical Analysis 2nd edition 2012

strategy_name: Breakout above a downtrend line with retest-of-new-support confirmation
mechanism: A prior resistance level becomes support after a break; a first retest that holds the broken line confirms the reversal, while a retest that breaches it exposes a 'fakeout'; longer-term trendlines dominate shorter-term ones.
setup_summary: Wait for the first break of a clearly defined downtrend line (long side), then wait for the first minor retracement; enter above the prior day's high only if the pullback holds above the broken line (new support); stop below the retest low. Canonical book variant: instrument bounces off a long-term (weekly/monthly) uptrend line, then breaks the intermediate-term downtrend line; entry on the break (often converging with the 50-day MA), stop below the break day's low; exit into resistance of the 50-day MA or a prior high (GLD, SMH, IBB, PBW trades).
trigger_invalidation: A retracement that pierces back below the broken line invalidates the reversal (fakeout); avoid first-break entries without retest confirmation ('blindly buying the first break').
risk_geometry: entry: above prior day's high after a holding retest, or on the break with MA convergence; stop: below retest low / break-day low; target: prior highs (reward/risk often 3-4:1, min 2:1); hold days to weeks.
quote: wait for the first minor retracement that follows. The idea is to make sure that the pullback does not breach new support of the prior downtrend line. If it does, the reversal attempt was likely a 'fakeout' to reel in the bulls.

strategy_name: Failed breakout to a new high -> reversal short
mechanism: A breakout that fails to hold traps breakout buyers; forced exits by trapped longs plus new shorts create a fast downside vacuum that often falls to the 50-day MA quickly.
setup_summary: Instrument makes a new high (ideally from a consolidation base) but holds it only briefly (book examples: 2 days) and closes back below the pivot; short the breakdown, or short the break of the 50-day MA after a one-day unconvincing bounce (XME). Intraday management: if a breakout entry is positioned to close the day below its pivotal resistance (wick above, body below on a daily candle), exit the same day - this marks a short/intermediate-term top, often after a stop hunt; a failed intraday breakout that follows through the next day can be reentered above the prior day's high. Gap-down below the pivot (DIA) is an especially bearish confirmation.
trigger_invalidation: Reclaim of the pivot (or rally above the head in the H&S analog) invalidates the short; failed breakouts in strongly-trending markets fail at higher rate and should be sized/held shorter.
risk_geometry: entry: break below pivot or below 50-day MA after failed bounce; stop: above pivot/head or above candle high (XME $65.82 above 10-day MA and down-candle high); target: prior low (e.g. June-14 low for MDY) or 50-day MA; short hold 1-5 days ('right or right out').
quote: Not only must all the bulls who bought the consolidation close the position, but those who bought the breakout must as well. This sudden exodus triggers a wave of downward momentum that, in turn, attracts the attention of short sellers.
chapter_anchor: Ch.7 breakout-failure discussion, Ch.8 'Strategies for Closing Losing Positions' (IWM Oct-2007, intraday rule), Ch.10 XME and DIA short trades
notes: Directly corroborates V8's failed_breakout expert (SHORT, close below windowed prior high); book adds the intraday close-below-pivot rule and the failed-breakdown mirror (bear trap) as refinements.

strategy_name: Head-and-shoulders top short with right-shoulder entry
mechanism: Traders trapped long at the head and left shoulder sell into the next rally (preventing a higher high and forming the right shoulder); when price returns to the neckline the trapped positions capitulate and the neckline break draws shorts into a momentum collapse. The predicted drop equals the head-to-neckline distance below the neckline.
setup_summary: Bearish H&S top (left shoulder + head + right shoulder + neckline) on any timeframe. Short during the right-shoulder formation (tight stop above the head, better reward/risk) or after a definitive neckline break (better confirmation, wider stop). Volume confirmation: lighter volume on the right shoulder than the left increases follow-through odds; rising right-shoulder volume is a warning. Target = head-to-neckline distance projected below the neckline (SPY 2002: ~10 points below ~$87 -> $77, hit exactly). Failure: rally above the head after the right shoulder = failed H&S with a powerful upward move (short squeeze + re-entry by shaken-out bulls) - a long setup. Timeframe-dependent completion: daily H&S takes weeks; hourly is more reliable in short-term bear phases. Book corroborates with a cross-market confirmation (hourly $OSX H&S + crude-oil lower high).
trigger_invalidation: Rally above the head invalidates the pattern (failed H&S -> strong counter-move); rising volume on the right shoulder warns of failure; stops must be respected until head/neckline levels are definitive.
risk_geometry: entry: mid-right-shoulder formation or neckline break; stop: just above the head (short) / below the head (inverse long); target: head-to-neckline distance below neckline, or next support (book covered OIH at 50-day MA support, $139, instead of the $133 target); expiry: timeframe-dependent (daily H&S = several weeks).
quote: My most profitable ETF short sales were often the result of capitalizing on this pattern... a relatively tight stop can be placed just over the top of the head, thereby creating much greater profit potential on a downward move than the risk of getting stopped out.
chapter_anchor: Ch.6 'Short Selling the Head-and-Shoulders Chart Pattern' (SPY 2002, IWM 2007) + Ch.10 OIH short (hourly $OSX H&S with crude lower high)
notes: Recognizable on 1h crypto charts but H&S reliability on 24/7 leveraged markets is unproven; the more robust, falsifiable sub-claims are the failed-H&S counter-move (connects to failed_breakout) and the neckline-measured-target rule.

strategy_name: Box range breakout with measured-move target
mechanism: consolidated box stores pent-up energy; a close-breakout projects a move at least equal to the vertical height of the box
setup_summary: Price trades inside a well-defined horizontal box range (Japanese 'box range', e.g., $50-$53) for an extended period; enter when a bar CLOSES outside the box (intraday penetration that does not close through leaves the level intact). Target = box height added to the broken boundary on the upside ($56) or subtracted on the downside ($47). Invalidation: a close back inside the box voids the target (change of polarity).
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: close outside a multi-touch box boundary. Thesis invalidated when price closes back inside the box (e.g., 'if the index had closed back above 3600, it would have voided my downside target of 2750'); mere intraday tag of the boundary does not break it.
risk_geometry: Entry at bar close on the breakout; target = box height projected from the broken boundary; invalidation = close back inside the box; targets are not stop/entry levels in their own right.
quote: When a breakout from box range unfolds, the market has good potential continuing in the direction of the breakout.
chapter_anchor: Ch 16, 'Breakouts from Boxes' (pp. 250-255, Exhibits 16.1-16.5)
notes: Corroborates and extends the DATA_BLOCKED breakout_retest backlog family with a falsifiable target rule (range-height projection) and a close-based invalidation. Crypto is dominated by lateral ranges; 24/7 no-gap closes make the close-break rule clean, but false breaks/liquidity sweeps are frequent, so the close-reclaim invalidation is load-bearing. Ascending/descending triangles (same chapter) are trended variants sharing the height-projection measurement.

strategy_name: Stochastic oversold + positive divergence + %K/%D cross with candle confirmation
mechanism: close near range low + divergence + fast/slow cross flags momentum turn; a candlestick pattern confirms the turn
setup_summary: After a decline: %D <= 20 (oversold), positive divergence (price lower low while stochastic makes a higher low), %K crosses above %D, and a bullish candlestick (e.g., hammer) confirms. Mirror for tops: %D >= 80, negative divergence, %K crossing under %D.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: %D<=20 + positive divergence + %K/%D bullish cross + candle confirmation. Invalidation: close below the confirming candle's low ('if the stock had pulled under the hammer's low then, in spite of the positive stochastic reading, one should consider vacating longs').
risk_geometry: Entry on the confirmed candle's close; stop under the signal candle's low; book gives no target or expiry (open-ended mean reversion).
quote: to get a buy signal, the market must be oversold (20% or less for %D), there is positive divergence, and the %K line is crossing above the %D line.
chapter_anchor: Ch 14, 'Using Stochastics' (pp. 233-237, Exhibits 14.6-14.7)
notes: Mean-reversion family — no active expert today; complexity budget caps at 3 actives, so this is a backlog candidate. Crypto 1h trends persist and oversold can stay sticky (liquidation cascades); must be gated by a trend-regime filter (see regime_filter) before screening.

strategy_name: Oscillator divergence confirmed by a reversal candle (exit/trim signal)
mechanism: price makes a new extreme while the oscillator (MA oscillator, stochastic, MACD) fails to confirm = momentum failure; a reversal candle converts divergence into an actionable signal
setup_summary: At a resistance/support area: price makes a new high (low) while the oscillator makes a lower high (higher low); a confirming bearish (bullish) candle (bearish engulfing, hanging man, shooting star) makes the signal actionable. Primary stated use: when a stock is overextended and a candlestick confirms a turn, exit or lighten longs; mirror for shorts.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: divergence + confirming candle. Invalidation: no candle confirmation = no signal ('we would not look to sell' on oscillator alone); hanging man requires a close under its real body next session for bearish confirmation.
risk_geometry: Exit/trim rule applied at overbought/oversold oscillator readings; confirmation and level breaks are close-based.
quote: at the time of that pattern the stock had made a new high and the moving average oscillator had made a lower high. This formed bearish or negative divergence.
chapter_anchor: Ch 14, Exhibit 14.5 (pp. 232-233); MACD section (pp. 237-239)
notes: Primary V8 value is an oscillator-divergence feature (windowed price extrema vs smoothed momentum extrema) in marketstate, consumed by other families as confirmation; the exit framing supports a lifecycle rule for trimming overextended positions. Divergence is noisy in crypto 1h and is treated here as confirmation, not a standalone entry.

strategy_name: Relative-volume confirmation of candle patterns and breakouts
mechanism: 'Volume is like water pressure in a hose': heavier volume on the confirming candle/breakout validates the price signal, while the setup candle should be relatively light
setup_summary: For any reversal/continuation candle pattern, check relative volume vs preceding sessions: a bullish engulfing/piercing pattern should show lighter volume on the first candle and heavier volume on the confirming candle; a hammer or rising-window break gains significance with a volume spike. Upside breakouts to new highs should be accompanied by a volume push — a low-volume new high is a reason to be circumspect. Volume should increase in the direction of the trend.
trigger_invalidation: Not a standalone trigger — a confirmation overlay. Adds no value on flat volume; low-volume breakout warrants caution but not a fade.
risk_geometry: No independent entry/stop/target; modulates aggressiveness (a high-volume hammer allows buying the close more aggressively because retracement to the hammer low is less likely).
quote: a bearish engulfing pattern should have a lighter volume on the first candle (the white) and a heavier volume on the second candle (the black) to increase the bearish engulfing pattern's significance.
notes: Maps to the 'participation' feature group. Crypto perp volume includes wash/manipulation noise and liquidation-driven spikes; use relative volume (quantile vs lookback), never absolute, exactly as the book advises. High value as a confirmation filter on candlestick families (engulfing, hammer, failed_breakout).

strategy_name: Flag/pennant and swing-target continuation with flagpole projection
mechanism: sharp impulse + short lateral/countertrend consolidation + resumption; measured target = flagpole height projected from the consolidation
setup_summary: A clean sharp advance (flagpole A to B) is followed by a short congestion band (flag = horizontal box; pennant = lower highs and higher lows), then price resumes the prior trend by breaking the consolidation. Target = flagpole height projected from the bottom of the band for longs (conservative) and from the top for shorts. Swing-target variant projects the first-leg channel height from the correction low/high.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: resumption break out of the consolidation following a defined impulse. Invalidation: the band resolves against the prior trend (e.g., bull flag breaks below flag support) or price closes back into the band.
risk_geometry: Entry on the resumption break; target = flagpole height from the bottom/top of the congestion band; stop = opposite side of the band.
quote: the height of the first leg is a rally from A to B. There is then a correction to C. Once the market ascends from C, we would 'swing' the initial channel height of A to B onto the correction low at C.
chapter_anchor: Ch 16, 'Swing Targets, Flags, and Pennants' (pp. 255-260)
notes: Continuation family. On crypto 1h the flagpole/consolidation structure is fuzzy; the falsifiable core is impulse -> range -> resumption with a projected target. Overlaps trend_pullback in spirit but differs by requiring a defined consolidation band and a measured objective.

strategy_name: Trend-regime gate on candle reversal signals
mechanism: a reversal candle's meaning is conditional on the larger trend regime; a bullish signal in a bear market is not a buy signal
setup_summary: Gate all candlestick reversal signals by the prevailing trend regime: a bullish candle pattern in a major bear market is not a buy signal, while a bullish formation confirmed by other technicals within a bull market is a buying point. 'Where you stand in relation to the overall technical evidence may be more important than an individual candle pattern.'
trigger_invalidation: N/A — a filter. Long setups with a bearish regime are skipped (or flagged for counter-trend study only); single-pattern signals without regime confirmation are not traded.
risk_geometry: No entry/stop/target of its own; modulates admission at the RiskGate.
quote: a bullish candle signal in a major bear market should not be used as a buy signal.
chapter_anchor: Conclusion (p. 268); Ch 17 convergence discussion (pp. 263-265)
notes: Directly supports a RiskGate/regime admission rule for counter-trend candle experts (e.g., stochastic/hammer mean-reversion setups). A 1h trend-regime classifier (EMA stack, higher-timeframe slope) is computable offline and deterministic.

strategy_name: Windows (gaps) as support/resistance
mechanism: a price void (window) acts as support (rising) or resistance (falling); closing the window damages the trend thesis
setup_summary: A rising window (gap up, entire range above the prior bar) is a bullish signal and should act as support; a falling window is a bearish signal and acts as resistance. High-volume windows are stronger levels. A close through the window confirms damage to the trend.
trigger_invalidation: The window level survives until price closes back through it; a close through voids it.
risk_geometry: Window = frozen level (support/resistance); break-and-close through it invalidates.
quote: When the market opens a window to the upside, it is a rising window. It is a bullish signal and the rising window should be support.
chapter_anchor: Glossary A, 'Windows' (p. 278); Ch 15 (Exhibit 15.3)
notes: 24/7 perp trading has no exchange gaps, so literal windows are rare (only whole-bar range discontinuities, e.g., around funding/listing events). The survivable core — prior session extremes as S/R — is already covered by the supply_demand_zone and sweep families. Reject the gap mechanic itself; optionally salvage a 'session-extreme level' feature.

strategy_name: Failed reclaim of broken 50-day MA (bounce into resistance)
mechanism: after a breakdown below a pivotal MA, the broken MA flips to resistance; a retracement that fails to reclaim it confirms downtrend resumption
setup_summary: Daily: price closes below its 50-day MA for the first time in months (also breaking the primary uptrend line), then retraces up to the MA and fails to reclaim it on two separate tests; short the following day on a break below the prior day's low.
trigger_invalidation: Trigger: two failed tests of the broken-MA resistance, then break below prior day's low. Invalidation: close back above the 50-day MA.
risk_geometry: Entry: break of prior day's low below established MA resistance. Stop: above the MA-resistance test high. Target: prior swing low, cover into weakness on the test. Expiry: days to ~2 weeks.
quote: In both tests, new resistance of the 50-day MA perfectly marked the highs of each day's rally
chapter_anchor: Ch. 10 'Bounce into Resistance of a 50-Day MA' (OIH)
notes: Distinct from failed_breakout: the reference level is a broken MA now acting as resistance and the setup is a failed reclaim of broken support (S/R flip), not a failed upside breakout of a prior high.
